analysis.one_liner: Loosens Dodd-Frank rules for banks, derivatives dealers, and small public companies.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 271-154 in January 2015, but the Senate Banking Committee never took it up, and the bill expired when that Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This package of Dodd-Frank changes would exempt commercial companies' non-cleared swaps from posting margin, delay until 2019 the date banks must divest certain pre-2014 collateralized loan obligations to comply with the Volcker Rule, exempt merger-and-acquisition brokers from SEC registration, spare small public companies from machine-readable XBRL filing, and ease registration for advisers to small-business investment companies. Supporters called it small-business regulatory relief; opponents said it peeled protections off the post-2008 financial rules. It passed the House but never received a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks holding pre-2014 collateralized loan obligations get three more years before Volcker Rule divestment; commercial swap users and swap dealers are spared margin requirements on non-cleared trades; merger brokers, small public companies, and private-fund advisers shed SEC registration and filing costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks, swap dealers, and small public companies

how_it_helps.text: Exempts swaps with commercial end users and certain affiliate trades from initial and variation margin requirements, lowering the cost of hedging business risk with non-cleared swaps.
Delays until July 21, 2019 the requirement that banks bring pre-2014 collateralized loan obligation holdings into Volcker Rule compliance.
Exempts certain merger-and-acquisition brokers from broker-dealer registration, while denying the exemption to brokers who hold customer funds or handle public offerings.
Exempts emerging growth companies and issuers with under $250 million in annual gross revenues from XBRL machine-readable reporting requirements, with an SEC cost-benefit study attached.
Repeals indemnification prerequisites so the CFTC and SEC can share swap data with other regulators, restoring the original Dodd-Frank information-sharing setup.
Doubles to $10 million the threshold below which companies selling employee-compensation securities must deliver extra disclosures to investors.

analysis.who_pays: Investors in small-company and emerging-growth stocks lose standardized machine-readable data; regulators lose margin coverage on a class of non-cleared swaps; the public bears whatever added credit risk those changes create.

drawbacks.text: Exempting commercial end-user swaps from margin requirements removes the posted collateral cushion that protects counterparties if a borrower defaults on a non-cleared trade.
The Volcker delay lets banks keep money tied up in pre-2014 collateralized loan obligations through mid-2019 rather than divesting them, leaving that exposure on bank balance sheets longer.
Exempting companies under $250 million in revenue from XBRL strips investors of the standardized, machine-readable financial data used to compare and monitor firms.
The bill directs the CFTC to implement its swap margin changes without the normal notice-and-comment process, using an interim final rule.
A Democratic amendment to bar people convicted of aiding terrorist organizations from the bill's new exemptions was rejected 183-242, along party lines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some provisions were widely accepted technical fixes: the indemnification repeal fixes a genuine information-sharing snag, the M&A broker exemption is hedged with real limits, and small-company filing relief has a plausible cost-benefit rationale. The ones with teeth for the financial sector are the margin exemption and the Volcker CLO delay, both of which shift risk away from regulated cushions. The savings to ordinary households are indirect at best, while the disclosure and margin protections given up are real, if modest.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 271-154 on January 14, 2015, but the Senate Banking Committee never took it up, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 6, 2015 and referred to the House Financial Services and Agriculture Committees.

A first attempt to pass it under suspension of the rules, which requires a two-thirds vote, failed on January 7, 2015 by 276-146, with 241 of 242 voting Republicans in favor and 145 of 185 Democrats opposed.
Republican leaders brought it back under a rule waiving points of order, and a Democratic motion to recommit it with an anti-terrorism amendment failed 183-242.
The House passed the bill on January 14, 2015, 271-154, with 242 of 245 Republicans and 29 of 188 Democrats voting yes.
The Senate received the bill on January 16, 2015 and referred it to the Banking Committee, where no further action ever occurred before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the Senate never acted, the Dodd-Frank margin, Volcker, and disclosure rules stayed in place, which favored investors and regulators; banks and swap dealers did not get the relief this bill offered, though similar provisions resurfaced in later Congresses.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and moved to suspend the rules and pass it on the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The fight ran mostly by party: the first vote failed with Republicans 241-1 for and Democrats 35-145 against, and final passage split 242-1 Republican yes versus 29-153 Democratic yes.

industries.industry: Large banks holding pre-2014 collateralized loan obligations
industries.note: The bill gives them until July 2019 to bring pre-2014 CLO debt holdings into Volcker Rule compliance, letting them keep those investments rather than sell them. The delay preserves bank profits while keeping the associated risk on bank balance sheets.

industries.industry: Swap dealers and commercial swap end users
industries.note: Exempting end-user and affiliate swaps from margin requirements lowers hedging costs for non-financial companies like energy firms, but also removes collateral cushions that would absorb losses if a counterparty defaults.

industries.industry: Small public companies and emerging growth companies
industries.note: They gain exemptions from XBRL machine-readable filing and looser pre-IPO disclosure rules, cutting compliance costs. The trade-off is that investors lose the standardized data those filings provided.

They are exempted from broker-dealer registration when facilitating sales of eligible private companies, reducing costs for brokers advising small-business owners. The exemption excludes brokers who take custody of client funds or handle public offerings.

industries.industry: Private fund and small-business investment company advisers
industries.note: Advisers to SBICs and venture-style funds are exempted from SEC registration and from state licensing requirements, reducing oversight of these investment managers.
